title: The problem may not be your marketing
description: Why a request for more content may point to an offer, message or evidence problem.

blocks.text: A company says it needs more content.
Sometimes it does.
But that request usually comes with an assumption:
the company already knows what needs to be said and only needs someone to package it.
That is where I like to slow things down.

Before discussing cameras, concepts or deliverables, I want to know why the current communication is not working. The answer might be marketing, but it could just as easily be the offer, the message or the lack of convincing evidence.
Those problems can look nearly identical from the outside.

A company with weak positioning may believe it needs more reach. A company with an unclear offer may believe it needs a better video. A company making unsupported claims may believe higher production value will make those claims more credible.
In each case, producing more content could make the company more visible without making it more convincing.
Marketing can only amplify what it is given
I generally look in four places.
First, does the audience understand what is being offered?
Second, can the company explain why it matters in language that makes sense outside its own walls?
Third, is there enough evidence to support what the company is claiming?
Finally, is the right message actually reaching the right people?
If the first three are unclear, increasing distribution usually multiplies the confusion.
That is why I do not start by asking what kind of video a company wants. I start by asking what the audience needs to understand, believe or do.
If people do not understand the product, the work needs explanation.
If they understand it but do not believe the claim, the work needs proof.
If they believe the claim but cannot picture the value, the work may need demonstration or story.
If all of that is working but no one sees it, then distribution may actually be the problem.
The format should come after that diagnosis.
We The Free started with a system problem
When We The Free began developing original programming, they were not trying to repair an existing content system. They were building one.
They knew they wanted original shows, but they did not yet have a complete framework for how those shows should be developed, produced and marketed in a way that strengthened the larger brand.

Working through Coyote Ranch, I became involved during that foundational stage. My role eventually covered creative development, cinematography, directing on selected episodes, editing, visual effects, audio, promotional material and live production.
The larger question was never simply, “How should this episode look?”

We had to think about how separate programs could have their own identities without feeling disconnected from We The Free. We also had to consider how the production process would support the show itself, its promotion and the continued growth of the platform.
That is a different job from showing up with a camera and executing a finished idea.
The questions that need answers
Before recommending production, I want to know:
What must the audience understand?
What are they likely to question?
What evidence do we actually have?
What decision should the communication support?
Where will the finished material be used?
These questions do not restrict the creative process. They keep the creative work attached to the reason the project exists.
They can also reveal that production is not the immediate answer.

Sometimes a company needs a campaign. Sometimes it needs a documentary, a series of interviews or a clear demonstration. Sometimes the message needs to be fixed before money is spent producing anything.
That is why I start with the problem, not the camera.

title: Trust is not a claim
description: How specific evidence helps an audience evaluate what a brand says.

blocks.text: Trust is one of those words brands love to put on websites.
Trusted. Experienced. Proven. Built for professionals. Committed to quality.
The problem is not that these claims are always false. The problem is that the audience has been given no reason to believe them.
A company cannot declare itself credible and expect the customer to finish the argument.
Trust develops when people can see enough evidence to reach that conclusion for themselves.
Every claim creates a question
Say a product is safer and the audience will ask how you know.
Say the company has a better process and people will want to know what is actually different.
Say the team is more experienced and they will look for the point where that experience becomes visible.
Those are reasonable questions. Good communication should answer them.
Weak communication often does something else. It repeats the claim more aggressively, puts it over expensive-looking footage and assumes polish will produce credibility.
It may produce attention. That is not the same thing.
I have seen beautiful work that tells me almost nothing about the company, the product or why I should believe what is being said. The production is technically good, but it never makes the case.
What does proof look like?
It depends on the claim.
Sometimes the audience needs to see the product performing.
Sometimes it needs to understand the process behind the result.
Sometimes the strongest evidence is hearing an experienced person explain a decision with enough specificity that the expertise becomes obvious.
Third-party validation can help as well: customers, collaborators, credentials, testing or recognition from a credible outside source.
The mistake is assuming one kind of proof works for everything.
If a manufacturer makes a performance claim, show the product working under relevant conditions.
If a company says its process produces a better result, explain the meaningful difference in that process.
If expertise is the advantage, stop asking people to describe themselves as experts. Ask them questions that allow the audience to hear how an expert thinks.
Specificity is usually more convincing than another adjective.
Production should make the evidence visible
I do not see production as decoration for the message. It should help prove the message.
That changes the questions we ask in an interview.
Instead of, “What makes your company different?” ask what the company does differently and why.
Instead of asking someone to say that quality matters, ask where quality is won or lost in the process.
Ask what commonly goes wrong. Ask what an experienced person notices that others miss. Ask which decisions are invisible to the customer but essential to the result.
Those answers contain evidence.

The same applies to the images. Do not show a facility simply because it looks impressive. Show what happens inside it that supports the claim. Do not photograph the product from ten attractive angles when one clear demonstration would say more.
A simple test
Take the most important claim on the page and ask:
What are we asking the audience to believe?
Why might a reasonable person hesitate?
What could we show that would answer that hesitation?
If there is no strong answer to the third question, the claim may be too broad or unsupported. That is worth discovering before production begins.
Confidence without evidence can become a liability. The harder a company pushes an unsupported statement, the more skeptical the audience may become.
A precise explanation is stronger than “industry-leading.”
A visible process is stronger than “quality.”
A demonstrated result is stronger than “trusted.”
Give people enough evidence and let them reach the conclusion.
That is where trust comes from.

title: Every asset needs a job
description: Plan production around the decision each piece of content needs to support.

blocks.text: One of the easiest ways to waste a production budget is to begin with a deliverable count.
Four videos. Twelve Reels. A new brand film. More footage for the library.
Those are outputs. They do not tell me what the material needs to accomplish.

A company can publish consistently and still fail to make its offer clearer. It can create polished work that never answers a customer’s concern. It can build an enormous footage library that no one knows how to use.
Before creating an asset, I want to know its job.
What makes an asset useful?
I need to know who it is for, what decision it should support, where people will encounter it and how long it needs to remain useful.
A short social video might earn attention but lack the room to explain a technical product.
A detailed customer interview might be extremely useful during consideration but too slow for initial discovery.
A brand film may establish context and confidence without being the right tool for direct response.
That does not make any of them bad assets. It means they serve different purposes.
Trouble starts when one video is expected to attract attention, explain the entire offer, prove every claim, answer objections and close the sale.
That is too much work for one piece of content.
Give each piece a defined role
A stronger system lets different assets handle different parts of the conversation.
One may introduce the problem.
Another may explain how the solution works.
A demonstration can provide proof.
A customer or subject-matter expert can address doubt.
A shorter edit can lead the audience toward the principal story.
The pieces should relate to one another, but they do not need to say the same thing in different aspect ratios.
Cropping the master video vertically is not a content strategy.
One production can keep working
I co-shot an episode involving Kentucky Ballistics and Ballistic Dummy Lab and contributed to the editorial work. Kentucky Ballistics later used my footage and edit to advertise the episode.
The promotional material did not replace the episode. It had a different job: give the audience a reason to watch it.
That experience reinforced something I already believed. The usefulness of production material does not have to end with the main deliverable.

A strong interview might support the principal story, a website section, a sales presentation, an email, and several focused edits. A demonstration may work inside the main film while also functioning as its own piece of proof.
But that only works consistently when those uses are considered before the shoot.
Otherwise, the production finishes and everyone starts digging through the footage, hoping something else can be made from it.
Sometimes it can. That is not the same as planning for it.
Plan backward
Before production, I want to know:
What is the main asset?
What question or objection does it address?
What supporting material will sales or marketing need?
Which moments deserve their own focused edit?
Where will each version appear?
What should remain useful after the initial release?
Those answers affect the interview questions, coverage, framing, still photography, audio, and the amount of context captured around the main story.
They also help determine what does not need to be filmed.
That part matters.
Efficiency is not measured by how many deliverables can be extracted from a shoot. It is measured by whether the production captures the material that has a real use.
More content is not automatically more leverage.
A smaller group of assets with defined jobs can be more valuable than months of disconnected posting.
Shoot less.
Make it mean more.
